- When sentiment is consistently negative or low (e.g., 0.00–0.33), model tends to over-forecast early spikes and under-forecast subsequent declines — apply downward bias correction to high-value forecast entries.
- After a sharp sentiment spike (e.g., 1.00–1.67), model often overreacts with exaggerated upward forecasts — cap or smooth out forecast peaks, especially in first 5–7 days.
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.33–0.67), model frequently underestimates mean reversion — adjust forecast by adding 10–20% of recent average to correct for lagged mean reversion.
- When sentiment is positive and forecast shows high volatility (e.g., >5x range), model tends to over-forecast downward corrections — apply a “sentiment-adjusted floor” to prevent excessive negative drift.
- For 30-day horizon, model often fails to capture short-term sentiment-driven reversals — use sentiment history to weight recent 3–5 day averages for smoothing and reducing overfitting to outliers.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “recovery” patterns (e.g., 0.33 → 1.00 → 0.33), model tends to over-forecast recovery — apply a “sentiment decay” multiplier (e.g., 0.8–0.9) to forecast entries following positive sentiment peaks.
